exam: What three clinical features most increase SUDEP risk? — Frequent generalized tonic‑clonic seizures, nocturnal seizures, and long epilepsy duration.

A 22‑year‑old with refractory epilepsy presents after a night‑time seizure; what immediate advice reduces SUDEP risk? — Arrange supervised sleeping, consider a seizure alarm, and optimise antiseizure therapy.
How does cardiac monitoring aid in SUDEP prevention? — Detects ictal arrhythmias; if found, treat with beta‑blockers or refer for electrophysiology evaluation.

Why is phenobarbital still a first‑line choice in low‑resource settings despite sedation risk? — It is inexpensive, widely available, and effective for generalized seizures; benefits outweigh sedation when monitored.
Differentiate SUDEP from status epilepticus in a post‑ictal patient. — SUDEP is a sudden death after a seizure; status epilepticus is ongoing seizure activity requiring emergent treatment.

What investigation would you order if EEG is unavailable and why? — Obtain a detailed seizure diary and clinical description to guide drug selection; this compensates for lack of electrophysiological data.
Explain why poly‑therapy may increase SUDEP risk. — Multiple drugs can cause additive side‑effects (e.g., cardiac conduction delay) and lower seizure threshold if not properly matched.

A patient on valproate develops liver dysfunction; how does this affect SUDEP risk? — Liver failure can worsen seizure control and increase metabolic instability, raising SUDEP risk; switch to an alternative agent.
ai.title: Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP)
related: Antiseizure drug selection in low‑resource settings
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: SUDEP is a fatal, non‑traumatic, non‑cardiac death occurring in people with epilepsy, usually during or shortly after a seizure. Risk is highest in uncontrolled generalized tonic‑clonic seizures and in low‑resource settings where monitoring and treatment gaps exist.

b: Occurs most often at night, during or after a generalized tonic‑clonic seizure
Incidence: 1‑2 per 1,000 patient‑years; higher in refractory epilepsy
sections.p: SUDEP describes a sudden, unexpected death in a person with epilepsy where autopsy shows no structural cause. It accounts for up to 20% of epilepsy mortality and is often preventable with optimal seizure control.

b: ≥3 generalized tonic‑clonic seizures per year markedly raises risk
Nocturnal seizures, young adult age, long epilepsy duration, and comorbid cardiac disease add risk
Use of poly‑therapy, especially with sodium channel blockers, may increase susceptibility
sections.p: Risk factors are stratified into seizure‑related, cardiac, respiratory and autonomic domains. The strongest predictor is the frequency of generalized tonic‑clonic seizures.

b: Identify high‑risk patients during routine clinic visits
Educate families about nocturnal supervision and seizure logs
Prioritise seizure control with affordable first‑line drugs (phenobarbital, carbamazepine, valproate) before adding newer agents
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, limited EEG, cardiac monitoring, and access to newer antiseizure medicines mean many patients remain uncontrolled, raising SUDEP risk.

t.b: Does the patient have ongoing epileptiform activity? → Confirms diagnosis and guides drug choice; if unavailable, rely on clinical seizure description.
Is there an underlying arrhythmia? → Detects cardiac channelopathies; if unavailable, obtain a resting ECG and consider referral.
Are electrolytes or glucose deranged? → Corrects reversible precipitants of seizures; if lab not available, use bedside glucometer and clinical assessment.

b: First‑line: phenobarbital, carbamazepine, or valproate – inexpensive, widely available, effective for most seizure types
Avoid drugs that lower seizure threshold (e.g., bupropion) and those with strong cardiac effects (e.g., high‑dose quinidine)
If refractory: consider referral for epilepsy surgery or vagus nerve stimulation where feasible
Educate on nocturnal supervision, use of seizure alarms, and safe sleeping environment
sections.p: Goal: achieve complete seizure freedom or at least eliminate generalized tonic‑clonic seizures.

b: Sudden cardiac death: primary cardiac cause, often with structural heart disease
Status epilepticus: prolonged seizure activity requiring emergent treatment, not a post‑ictal death
sections.p: Sudden cardiac death, status epilepticus, and accidental injury during a seizure.

b: Absence of post‑ictal apnea on bedside observation does not guarantee safety; apnea may be brief and unnoticed
sections.p: Normal post‑mortem findings do not exclude SUDEP; a negative ECG does not rule out intermittent arrhythmias during seizures.

whenToSeekHelp: Any patient with epilepsy who experiences a generalized tonic‑clonic seizure lasting >5 minutes
New onset of nocturnal seizures or sudden change in seizure pattern
Witnessed post‑ictal apnea or loss of consciousness lasting >10 minutes
